name: Yusuf Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and isn't linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior composer at Bluebridge Audio, a five-person studio that makes music and sound effects for mobile games. Today it was forty seconds of happy loop music for a farming game and about thirty coin sounds, each one slightly different. My boss, Lena, sends the brief in the morning and I've got it to her by four. Weekends I play oud and guitar at family weddings and community events, which is where I actually learned to play.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI in the studio?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, all day. I generate rough loops, use AI to clean up sound effects, and have a chatbot help me write the cue lists the game developers want. Honestly, I'm not as skilled as the senior composer, Marco, so the tools let me keep up. I share a flat with my cousin Idris and have about four months saved. I'd like my own studio one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and the people who use them well will do best. That's how markets work. I'd post a short video showing how I make a game loop in an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things stay good for me. Bluebridge has steady clients and I'm getting faster. I'd stay a couple more years and learn the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep learning the tools, and save towards my own studio. I'd ask Lena if I can sit in on client calls to learn how she wins work. I'd keep the weekend weddings for extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually optimistic. It's a good picture for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your own studio look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small, just me and maybe one other, doing music for games and for families' wedding videos. I'd build a studio that makes game music on weekdays and wedding films for my own community on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you need saved before going it alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a year's costs, I'd say. I'm at four months. With Idris splitting rent, maybe two more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, and I'd mean it kindly. Studios that use AI will win the contracts. I wouldn't ask the government to stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job at Bluebridge is at risk. If the developers can generate their own coin sounds, they need Lena and Marco, not me. I'm the easiest one to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own small business sooner, maybe within the year, offering fast AI-assisted music for indie game developers. I'd keep the weekend wedding work because that's people, not screens. I'd learn the newest tools before anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the job, excited about the business. Both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't starting a business on four months of savings risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. But Idris would carry rent for a few months, and my uncle has said he'd lend me a bit. Four months of savings and an uncle who believes in me is more start-up money than most studios had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would your first clients be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small indie game makers on online forums, people who can't afford Bluebridge. I'd charge less and deliver in two days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will need each other more than ever. I'd also say people should stay calm and not expect the state to fix everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, game audio is all screen work. By 2028 a game maker types what they want and gets the whole soundtrack in seconds. My job and my business plan both go. Only the live oud playing at weddings has time, until the robots in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the business plan and protect my savings. I'd play every wedding and community event I can. I'd look at learning a hands-on trade, maybe electrical work, because someone has to wire the buildings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lose the career I've been building, and the plan B, at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I need to switch quickly and I might need help. My dad would tell me to come and work at his shop. My dad has offered me a job at his phone repair shop since I was sixteen, and in this picture I'd finally say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that feel like failure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But my dad's shop has fed our family for twenty years. There's no shame in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for businesses to adapt and for people to learn new skills. I'd say opportunity is there for people who move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me run my business for a few years, using AI to do the work of five people. After 2031 the screen part goes, but I'd have savings and clients by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the business next year, keep costs low, and save hard. I'd also learn something hands-on, maybe installing sound systems in venues, which buys me until 2034. I'd keep the weddings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way that keeps me moving. Five years is a race I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sound installation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's hands-on, and I understand audio already. A computer can write a whole soundtrack, but somebody still has to hang the speakers in a wedding hall and run the cables.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell other junior composers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use the tools, build your own clients, and learn a trade on the side. Don't wait for a studio to save you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to work. Build skills, build businesses, look after family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a gift for someone like me. I could build a proper studio, hire someone, and make good money before AGI arrives. By 2036 I'd want a business with a physical side, like installing sound systems, that robots don't reach till 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the studio in a year, invest in good equipment and learn every AI tool going. I'd add sound installation for wedding halls and community centres by year three. I'd save and maybe buy a small studio space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly hopeful. A decade's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd marry. My mother has opinions about that. With ten years of warning, I'd build a business my children could walk into, not just a job a computer takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. Starting a studio on four months of savings at twenty-seven is either brave or stupid, and ten years gives me time to find out which.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose my job and my business plan before either got going. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses and short trade courses, so young people can switch fast without waiting for a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about community. At weddings, people want the oud played by someone they know. That's not going away, even if the money in it is small.

headlineQuote: With ten years of warning, I'd build a business my children could walk into, not just a job a computer takes.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old junior composer** at a small game audio studio who plays oud at family weddings.
He uses **AI tools all day**, shares a flat with his cousin and has about four months saved.
He's **traditional and adaptive**, dreams of his own studio and resists relying on the state.
He expects to be the **first cut** at the studio and turns that into a business plan.
When time is short, he'd fall back on his **dad's phone repair shop**, with no shame.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd lose his job and business plan **together**.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **small-business loans** and short **trade courses** for fast switching.
